course.title: Sensitization on Drug Use, Drug Dependence and Drug Prevention, Treatment and Care (DPTC)
course.summary: The Drug Prevention, Treatment and Care (DPTC) sensitization course adapts the UNODC/European Union-supported “Response to Drugs and Related Organised Crime in Nigeria” trainer resource for self-paced online delivery by KADSAMHSA (Kaduna State Ministry of Health / Kaduna State Agency for the Control of AIDS, Drug Abuse and Substance Use). Across 13 modules it equips law enforcement officers, health workers, social workers and community leaders across Kaduna State to understand why people use drugs, distinguish use from dependence, reduce stigma at first contact, and refer people toward evidence-based treatment and care rather than punishment alone. Each module opens with an ungraded pre-test, moves through short content lessons with an embedded knowledge check and a discussion-based case study, and closes with a graded post-test (pass mark 80%); a 26-question final assessment covers the full curriculum.

lessons.title: Introduction and Course Outline
lessons.main:
Start here: why this course exists, what sensitization means, and how the course works
Adapted for online delivery by KADSAMHSA from the UNODC/European Union Trainer Resource Modules, “Response to Drugs and Related Organised Crime in Nigeria” (May 2019).

lessons.title: Learning Objectives
lessons.main:
By the end of this module, you will be able to:
1. Explain that risk of drug use is associated with multiple factors, most outside the individual's control
2. Distinguish between drug use prevention and sensitization, and explain how they complement each other
3. Describe the aims of DPTC sensitization: increasing knowledge and reducing stigma
4. Outline the topics, learning methods and expectations of the DPTC course

Pre-Test — Check Your Starting Point (not graded)

Q1. The strongest evidence about why people begin using drugs points to:
A. A simple lack of knowledge about drugs and their consequences
B. Multiple risk factors including personality, mental health, family and community environment
C. Deliberate moral failure by the individual
D. Exposure to drug education campaigns
Q2. The primary objective of drug use prevention is to:
A. Punish those who use drugs
B. Help people avoid or delay initiation of drug use, or avoid developing disorders
C. Eliminate all drugs from society
D. Identify drug users for arrest
Q3. Sensitization on drug use and DPTC primarily aims to:
A. Teach people how to use drugs safely
B. Increase knowledge and awareness, and reduce stigma
C. Replace drug treatment services
D. Train law enforcement in drug interdiction
Q4. Most of the risk factors that make a child vulnerable to drug use are:
A. Fully within the child's control
B. Largely outside the child's control
C. Caused by drug education in schools
D. Genetic only
Q5. In recent years, the global response to drug use disorders has increasingly treated them as:
A. Exclusively a criminal and legal matter
B. A health issue requiring evidence-based treatment and prevention
C. A private family matter
D. An issue with no effective response

lessons.title: Why This Course Exists
lessons.main:
BACKGROUND

UNODC assessments in Nigeria examined attitudes to drug prevention, treatment and care (DPTC) among law enforcement and the public
Finding: a clear need to raise the profile of sensitization on the nature of drug use, drug dependence and DPTC
The sensitization course aims to:
Increase knowledge and awareness of drug use, dependence and DPTC
Reduce the stigma associated with drug use
Longer-term impact: evidence-based policy, evidence-based services, and improved service uptake
KADSAMHSA has adopted this package for online delivery to build workforce and community capacity across Kaduna State

lessons.title: What This Module Covers
lessons.main:
Risk factors for drug use
Prevention of drug use
Understanding sensitization
Brief overview of the course outline, learning methods and expectations

lessons.title: Risk Factors for Drug Use
lessons.main:
MORE THAN A LACK OF KNOWLEDGE

It was once thought that better information alone would stop drug use — evidence shows otherwise
Dominant risk factors identified by international research:
Personality traits (sensation-seeking, aggressive, impulsive)
Mental health disorders
Family neglect and abuse; abusive parenting; chaotic home environment
Poor attachment to school and community; negative school environment
Growing up in marginalized and deprived communities
Source: International Standards on Drug Use Prevention, UNODC, 2013

lessons.title: Most Risk Factors Are Outside the Child's Control
lessons.main:
No child chooses to be neglected by their parents
Marginalized youth in poor communities — with little family support and limited education — are especially at risk
Children and communities affected by conflict or disaster face elevated risk
Risky behaviours (dropping out, aggression, delinquency, risky sex, depression) often share a health-disorder dimension
Blaming the individual displays a lack of understanding of what leads people to use drugs

Knowledge Check

A colleague says: “If young people just knew the dangers, they would not use drugs.” What does the evidence say?
A. Correct — information alone prevents drug use
B. Incorrect — risk is driven by multiple personal, family and community factors beyond knowledge
C. Correct — but only for cannabis
D. Incorrect — drug use is purely genetic

Answer: B — Information-only approaches show little or no lasting behaviour change.

lessons.title: What Is Prevention?
lessons.main:
Primary objective: help people — particularly young people — avoid or delay initiation of drug use, or avoid developing disorders (e.g. dependence)
The broader aim: the healthy and safe development of children and youth so they realize their talents and become contributing members of society
Effective prevention supports positive engagement with family, school, workplace and community
Evidence-based programmes go beyond information — they address the risk factors that contribute to drug use
Source: International Standards on Drug Use Prevention, UNODC, 2013

lessons.title: What Is Sensitization?
lessons.main:
An educational approach to inform, illuminate and challenge pre-existing ideas about drug use, dependence and DPTC
Aims: increase knowledge and awareness; reduce stigma associated with drug use
Targets local leaders and practitioners to:
Gain their endorsement and support for DPTC interventions
Increase their understanding of drug use as a health issue — not just a criminal or legal issue
Guided by the latest international scientific evidence to ensure credibility and validity

lessons.title: Sensitization and Prevention: Complementary but Different
lessons.main:
Prevention

Aim: avoid or delay initiation of drug use; prevent progression to disorders
Primary target: children, young people, families, schools, communities
Outcome: reduced initiation and reduced vulnerability
Strategy: evidence-based programmes addressing risk and protective factors

Sensitization

Aim: increase knowledge and reduce stigma about drug use, dependence and DPTC
Primary target: local leaders, practitioners, law enforcement, the public
Outcome: endorsement of DPTC; drug use understood as a health issue
Strategy: education grounded in current international scientific evidence

lessons.title: Course Outline: What You Will Study
lessons.main:
Foundation modules (1–5):
The drug use situation in Nigeria
Supply reduction
Demand and harm reduction
Drugs, effects and dependency
Causes of drug use and stigma
Treatment and care modules (6–9):
Types of drug treatment
Special populations
Drug screening (ASSIST)
Advocacy
Systems and rights modules (10–12):
Family interventions
Human rights and drug users
Specific issues for law enforcement
Each topic is a self-contained online module; complete them in the sequence assigned by your programme coordinator

lessons.title: How the Online Course Works
lessons.main:
Each module includes: a pre-test, content slides, knowledge checks, a case study, additional readings, and a post-test
Pre-test: sets your baseline — it is not graded
Post-test: pass mark is 80% (4 of 5); you may retake after reviewing the module
Case studies: respond in the LMS discussion forum where indicated
Short films are provided as viewing links, and group activities are delivered as LMS forum discussions

lessons.title: Online Learning Agreement
lessons.main:
State opinions honestly in forums so everyone benefits from frank discussion
Ask clarifying questions freely through the LMS discussion boards or help desk
Listen to (read) a person's full opinion before reacting — discuss ideas, not the person expressing them
Unpopular opinions may be expressed respectfully — we learn from them
Work to resolve disagreements rather than taking inflexible positions
Complete modules and assessments within the timelines set by your programme coordinator

lessons.title: Introduce Yourself (Icebreaker — LMS Forum Activity)
lessons.main:
Post a short introduction in the Module 0 forum:
My full name is…
I am from the following organisation/agency, and my designation is…
Briefly, what I would like to gain from this course is…
One good thing that happened to me in the past year was…
Read and reply to at least two other participants — you will be working alongside them throughout the course

lessons.title: Reframing Drug Use in the Community
lessons.main:
A respected community leader in a Kaduna LGA tells a KADSAMHSA outreach team: “The only way to deal with these drug boys is to hand them to the police. Talking about ‘health’ will just encourage them.”
The outreach team has 15 minutes with the leader and a group of ward heads. They want the leader's endorsement for a planned community sensitization programme and referral pathway to a PHC Centre of Excellence.

Discuss / respond in the LMS forum:

What key messages from this module would you use with the leader?
How would you explain the difference between sensitization and ‘encouraging’ drug use?
Which risk factors would you highlight to shift blame away from the individual?
What would you ask the leader to actually do to show endorsement?

lessons.title: Key Points of this Module
lessons.main:
1. Risk of drug use is driven by multiple factors — most outside the individual's control
2. Prevention helps people avoid or delay drug use; its broader aim is healthy, safe development
3. Sensitization increases knowledge and reduces stigma, targeting leaders and practitioners
4. Drug use is a health issue, not only a criminal or legal issue
5. This course is evidence-based and each module is a self-contained online unit

modules.title: The Drug Use Situation in Nigeria

lessons.title: The Drug Use Situation in Nigeria
lessons.main:
Online self-paced module with pre-test, knowledge checks, case study and post-test
Adapted for online delivery by KADSAMHSA from the UNODC/European Union Trainer Resource Modules, “Response to Drugs and Related Organised Crime in Nigeria” (May 2019).

lessons.title: Learning Objectives
lessons.main:
By the end of this module, you will be able to:
1. Describe the three components of the National Survey on Drug Use and Health (2018)
2. Summarize major drug supply issues in Nigeria, including trafficked drugs and precursors
3. Describe the extent and patterns of drug use in Nigeria by gender, age and drug type
4. Explain the health consequences of high-risk drug use, including blood-borne viruses
5. Identify the major barriers to accessing drug treatment in Nigeria
6. Describe drug use and criminal justice implications, and suggested policy responses

Pre-Test — Check Your Starting Point (not graded)

Q1. In 2017, the estimated past-year prevalence of drug use (excluding alcohol and tobacco) among Nigerians aged 15–64 was:
A. 5.6%
B. 14.4%
C. 22.4%
D. 2.1%
Q2. Which geopolitical zone had the highest drug use prevalence in the 2018 survey?
A. North-Central
B. North-West
C. South-West
D. South-South
Q3. Nearly what proportion of high-risk drug users in Nigeria are opioid users?
A. 10%
B. 25%
C. 50%
D. 90%
Q4. Which of these was identified as a key barrier to drug treatment in Nigeria?
A. Too many treatment centres
B. Prohibitive cost, stigma and lack of available services
C. Free universal treatment
D. Excess treatment information
Q5. In the past 12 months before the survey, what share of high-risk drug users had received treatment for a drug problem?
A. 4%
B. 24%
C. 44%
D. 64%

lessons.title: Drug Supply: Nigeria as a Transit and Production Point
lessons.main:
SUPPLY CONTEXT

West Africa, including Nigeria, remains a key transit point for drug trafficking
Trafficked substances: cannabis, cocaine, precursors (ephedrine for ATS manufacture) and tramadol
Late 2017: Lagos customs seized 115 tons of tramadol
Cocaine: Nigeria a major trafficking hub and transit country within West Africa
Cannabis: cultivation well established, concentrated in the South-West; the main drug seized by NDLEA
ATS: since 2011, 12 methamphetamine laboratories dismantled; 2016 ‘super lab’ could produce 3,000 kg per cycle; 1,352 kg seized in 2016
Precursors: 718 kg of ephedrine seized in 2016; 168 kg in 2017; diversion of legally imported ephedrine remains a concern
Source: NDLEA seizure data; UNODC World Drug Report 2017/2018

lessons.title: The National Survey on Drug Use and Health (2018)
lessons.main:
Nigeria's first large-scale, comprehensive, nationwide drug use survey
Conducted by NBS and CRISA with UNODC technical support; funded by the EU (10th EDF)
Three components:
National Household Survey: 38,850 households, rural and urban
Interviews with 9,344 problem drug users
Key Informant Survey: 2,787 persons
Coverage: all 36 states and the FCT; survey period 2016–2017

lessons.title: The Extent of Drug Use in Nigeria
lessons.main:
An estimated 14.3 million people aged 15–64 used drugs (excluding alcohol and tobacco) in 2017
Around one in seven adults — more than double the global average
Many people using drugs used more than one substance in the past year

Drug use in Nigeria is significantly high and a concern for all

14.4%
of Nigerians aged 15–64 used a drug in the past year (2017) — vs a 5.6% global average (2016)
Source: Drug Use in Nigeria 2018 (UNODC/NBS/CRISA)

lessons.title: Who Uses Drugs? Gender and Age
lessons.main:
An estimated 10.8 million men and 3.4 million women reported past-year drug use
One in four drug users in Nigeria is a woman (globally: one in three)
Highest levels of past-year use: ages 25–39; lowest: below 24
Amphetamines and ecstasy: more common among young people
Non-medical use of pharmaceutical opioids and cough syrup: found among older people (45–64)

lessons.title: High-Risk Drug Users and Injecting
lessons.main:
High-risk drug user: used opioids, crack/cocaine or amphetamines in past 12 months AND at least 5 times in the past 30 days
Estimated ~376,000 high-risk drug users (0.4% of the population); nearly 90% are opioid users
About 80,000 people had injected drugs — roughly one in five high-risk users injects
Most common drugs injected: pharmaceutical opioids, then cocaine and heroin (75% inject opioids)
78% of PWID are men, but women were more likely to inject heroin
Nearly half of PWID reported using a needle/syringe after someone else — women more likely to share a partner's equipment

lessons.title: Health Consequences: Infections and Poly-Drug Use
lessons.main:
Around 6% of high-risk drug users self-reported living with HIV; ~9% of PWID
2014 IBBSS bio-behavioural data (6 states): 3.4% of PWID living with HIV
Injecting is associated with HIV, hepatitis B and C, overdose and injection-site infections
Poly-drug use: 95% of high-risk users used more than one substance in the past year (42% among general-population users)
In Nigeria, more than 80% of high-risk drug users show dependence severity requiring some intervention

lessons.title: Drug Use by Geopolitical Zone (2017)
lessons.main:
North-Central: 10.0% — lowest prevalence (~1.5 million users; cannabis, cough syrup, opioids)
North-West (includes Kaduna State): 12.0% — cannabis by far the most used, then opioids and cough syrup
North-East: 13.6% — cannabis widely used, followed closely by opioids
South-West: 22.4% — highest in the country (cannabis, opioids, cough syrup ~700,000, tranquilizers ~207,000)
South-South: 16.6% — cannabis and opioids the main drugs
Planning point: KADSAMHSA programmes serve a zone where cannabis and opioids dominate the treatment demand profile
Source: Drug Use in Nigeria 2018

Knowledge Check

One in how many high-risk drug users in Nigeria injects drugs?
A. One in two
B. One in five
C. One in twenty
D. One in fifty

Answer: B — ~80,000 PWID among ~376,000 high-risk users.

lessons.title: Treatment Access and Barriers
lessons.main:
Treatment is mainly in tertiary hospitals, some NGOs and faith-based centres; services are not free
Key barriers:
Prohibitive cost
Fear and social stigma
Treatment not available
No information on where to find local treatment
Yobe, Imo, Bayelsa, Rivers and Lagos ranked hardest states to access treatment

4%

of high-risk drug users received treatment in the past 12 months; only 12% ever received treatment

lessons.title: Social and Criminal Justice Consequences
lessons.main:
Two-thirds of general-population drug users reported missing school/work, poor performance, or neglecting family
Nearly 1 in 8 Nigerian adults has suffered consequences from another person's drug use
Nearly one quarter of high-risk users had ever been arrested for a drug-related offence; ~9% in the past year
Of those arrested: 73% for possession; also theft (12%), sex work (5%), burglary (4%)

lessons.title: The National Response: Achievements to Date
lessons.main:
UNODC/EU project ‘Response to Drugs and Related Organised Crime in Nigeria’ (2013–2019)
National Drug Control Master Plan 2015–2019: development, implementation and monitoring supported
National Minimum Standards for Drug Treatment in Nigeria (2018)
National guidelines on estimation and quantification of narcotics and precursors for medical/scientific purposes
Drug treatment training for over 1,200 health practitioners
11 model drug treatment centres and 7 regional training centres established; Nigerian Epidemiological Network created

lessons.title: Using Survey Data for State-Level Planning
lessons.main:
You are preparing a briefing for the Kaduna State Ministry of Health budget committee. A committee member argues that scarce funds should go to interdiction only, saying: “Treatment is a federal problem — and anyway, hardly anyone here uses drugs.”
You have the 2018 national survey at hand: North-West prevalence of 12%, cannabis and opioid dominance, a 4% past-year treatment rate among high-risk users, and cost/stigma/availability as the leading barriers.

Discuss / respond in the LMS forum:

Which three statistics would you lead with, and why?
How does the treatment gap argument support investment in KADSAMHSA services (e.g., PHC-level care)?
How would you respond to ‘hardly anyone here uses drugs’ using zone-level data?
What one policy recommendation would you make based on the barriers identified?

lessons.title: Key Points of this Module
lessons.main:
1. 14.4% of Nigerians aged 15–64 used drugs in 2017 — over twice the global average
2. Cannabis and (non-medical) opioids, especially tramadol, dominate the pattern of use
3. About 376,000 high-risk users; ~80,000 inject; sharing of injecting equipment is common
4. Only 4% of high-risk users accessed treatment in the past year — cost, stigma and availability are the key barriers
5. Drug use carries heavy social and criminal justice consequences; policy responses must widen affordable treatment

modules.title: Understanding the Concept of Supply Reduction

lessons.title: Understanding the Concept of Supply Reduction
lessons.main:
Online self-paced module with pre-test, knowledge checks, case study and post-test
Adapted for online delivery by KADSAMHSA from the UNODC/European Union Trainer Resource Modules, “Response to Drugs and Related Organised Crime in Nigeria” (May 2019).

lessons.title: Learning Objectives
lessons.main:
By the end of this module, you will be able to:
1. Describe the global scale and patterns of drug use, cultivation and trafficking
2. Define supply reduction and identify its main methods
3. Explain the three strategic pillars: supply reduction, demand reduction and harm reduction
4. Critically assess the challenges and limitations of supply reduction
5. Describe alternative development and the conditions for its success

Pre-Test — Check Your Starting Point (not graded)

Q1. Roughly how many people worldwide used illicit drugs in 2016?
A. 27 million
B. 275 million
C. 2.75 billion
D. 755 million
Q2. Supply reduction is best defined as:
A. Reducing the desire to use drugs through education
B. Methods to reduce or stop production and trafficking of illicit drugs before they reach consumers
C. Providing clean needles to PWID
D. Treating drug dependence with medication
Q3. Cannabis use prevalence in West and Central Africa compared with the global average is:
A. Much lower
B. About the same
C. Much higher (13.2% vs 3.9%)
D. Zero
Q4. Seventeen years of opium eradication data in Afghanistan show that eradication:
A. Ended opium cultivation
B. Failed to keep pace with cultivation despite huge resources
C. Was never attempted
D. Reduced global heroin purity
Q5. In the cocaine value chain example, 1 kg of paste worth $585 in the Colombian jungle can ultimately retail on US streets for about:
A. $5,000
B. $27,000
C. $330,000 (after adulteration to 2 kg)
D. $1,000,000

lessons.title: A Drug-Using World
lessons.main:
Just over a quarter of a billion people used illicit drugs in 2016
Including legal drugs (alcohol, tobacco) the figure would be substantially higher
Drug use increased by around 20 million people between 2015 and 2016

275m

people aged 15–64 used illicit drugs in 2016 — about 1 in 18 adults (5.6% prevalence)
Source: UNODC World Drug Report 2018

lessons.title: Key Types of Drugs Used Globally
lessons.main:
Opioids: ~34 million users — includes opiates and synthetic analogues (fentanyl, methadone, buprenorphine, tramadol)
Opiates: ~19 million users — naturally derived (opium, morphine, codeine) and semi-synthetics such as heroin
Africa, including Nigeria, is a transit area for Afghan heroin — driving increased local heroin use
Cannabis in Africa: 7.6% prevalence vs 3.9% globally; West/Central Africa: 13.2%
Methamphetamine (an ATS) rising in many regions, especially Asia
PWID worldwide: ~11 million (2016); China, Russia and the USA host 45% of them; injecting now documented in 36 sub-Saharan African countries including Nigeria

lessons.title: Where Drugs Are Cultivated and Produced
lessons.main:
Opium poppy (heroin, opium, opiates): South-West Asia (Afghanistan) and South-East Asia (Lao PDR, Myanmar)
Coca bush (cocaine): South America
Cannabis: resin — North Africa, Middle East, South-West Asia; herb — grown globally (including Nigeria)
Amphetamine-type stimulants: manufactured in all regions of the world
Trafficking routes constantly change with production shifts and law enforcement pressure

lessons.title: Three Strategic Solutions to the World Drug Problem
lessons.main:
Supply reduction: disrupt production and supply of illicit drugs; control and regulate licit substances
Demand reduction: prevent uptake of harmful drug use, including abstinence-oriented strategies (Module 3)
Harm reduction: reduce drug-related harm to individuals and communities (Module 3)
A balanced drug policy uses all three — no single pillar succeeds alone

lessons.title: Supply Reduction: Methods
lessons.main:
Eradicate cultivation of crops used for illicit drugs (coca, opium poppy)
Target and dismantle clandestine laboratories (e.g., ATS ‘super labs’)
Seize drugs and interdict trafficking by land, air and sea; arrest traffickers
Regulate licit substances: laws and controls on alcohol, tobacco, pharmaceuticals, over-the-counter medicines and inhalants

Reality check: seizures have not matched large-scale cultivation and production

Source: UNODC 2015

lessons.title: Challenges of Supply Reduction
lessons.main:
Fully effective only when demand is low and all countries cooperate
High global cost — estimated around US$100 billion per year
Cultivation zones are often remote, politically unstable or outside central government control
Drug income funds militias, organized crime and other illegal activity
Legal crops often cannot compete with illicit crop profits
Eradication frequently displaces production elsewhere (the ‘balloon effect’)
Afghanistan: 17 years of eradication failed to keep pace with cultivation

lessons.title: Follow the Money: Profit and Corruption
lessons.main:
Cocaine value chain (OAS 2013): $585/kg paste in the Colombian jungle → $5,000 at port → $15,000 at the Mexican border → $27,000 entering the US → adulterated to 2 kg → ~$330,000 on the street
Estimated global drug-related income: US$426–652 billion (2014)
“Drug cartels buy more than real estate, banks and businesses; they buy elections, candidates and parties. In a word, they buy power.” — Antonio Maria Costa, former UNODC Executive Director (2008)
US example: drug control budget rose past US$23 billion (1981–2002), yet street heroin purity rose and price fell

Knowledge Check

Why does eradicating drug crops in one area often fail to reduce overall supply?
A. Farmers stop growing all crops
B. Production shifts elsewhere — the ‘balloon effect’ — while profits still outcompete legal crops
C. Eradication is illegal under international law
D. Drug crops cannot be destroyed

Answer: B

lessons.title: Alternative Development
lessons.main:
Illicit crops give farmers quick returns from non-perishable products — survival income, but no long-term development
Alternative development targets the vulnerabilities and poverty that draw communities into illicit cultivation
Combines viable legal livelihoods, infrastructure, market access and community development
Key challenges: long-term financial investment and sustained political commitment
Source: UNODC 2015

lessons.title: The Tramadol Seizure Dilemma
lessons.main:
A joint operation in a northern commercial hub seizes a container of tramadol tablets falsely declared as vitamins. Interviews reveal an established route feeding markets across several states, with demand strongest among transport workers and out-of-school youth.
At the debrief, one officer proposes doubling checkpoint seizures. A public health adviser notes that seizures have risen for years while non-medical tramadol use has also risen.

Discuss / respond in the LMS forum:

Using this module, explain why seizures alone are unlikely to solve the tramadol problem.
Which demand-side factors keep the market profitable despite interdiction?
Tramadol also has legitimate medical uses — what regulatory (licit supply control) issues does this raise?
Draft one balanced recommendation combining supply reduction with another pillar.

lessons.title: Key Points of this Module

2. Supply reduction targets production and trafficking before drugs reach consumers
3. Eradication, lab dismantling and seizures have not kept pace with production; profits fuel corruption
4. Supply reduction also includes regulating legal substances such as alcohol, tobacco and pharmaceuticals
5. Supply reduction works best as one pillar of a balanced strategy with demand and harm reduction

lessons.title: Learning Objectives
lessons.main:
By the end of this module, you will be able to:
1. Define demand reduction and describe its main components
2. Describe evidence-based prevention interventions across family, school and community settings
3. Explain what makes school-based drug education effective — and what does not work
4. Define harm reduction and explain its rationale and practical logic
5. List the ten interventions of the WHO/UNODC/UNAIDS comprehensive harm reduction package

Pre-Test — Check Your Starting Point (not graded)

Q1. Demand reduction means:
A. Seizing drugs at borders
B. Reducing the demand or need for drugs through prevention, education, treatment and social support
C. Reducing drug prices
D. Closing pharmacies
Q2. Which school-based approach does evidence support?
A. Scare tactics highlighting dangers
B. One-off talks by strangers such as police or 'recovered users'
C. Multiple short sessions integrated into the usual curriculum, delivered by the usual teacher
D. Sensational materials
Q3. Harm reduction primarily aims to:
A. Encourage drug use
B. Reduce the health, social and economic harms associated with drug use
C. Replace all treatment
D. Punish relapse
Q4. The motorbike helmet is used in this module as an analogy for:
A. Supply reduction
B. Harm reduction — reducing consequences without condoning the risk behaviour
C. Crop eradication
D. Drug testing
Q5. Which intervention belongs to the comprehensive harm reduction package?
A. Needle and syringe programmes
B. Mandatory detention
C. Public shaming
D. Crop spraying

lessons.title: What Is Demand Reduction?
lessons.main:
Reducing the demand or need for illicit drugs through prevention, education, treatment and social support programmes
Education and information: general community, youth (school and non-school), and people who use drugs
Treatment: detoxification, counselling, rehabilitation, therapeutic community, substitution therapy, social reintegration
Community development: address poverty and socio-economic drivers; integrate people into meaningful social structures

lessons.title: Prevention Within Demand Reduction
lessons.main:
Any activity focused on preventing or delaying initiation of drug use and the transition to problem use
Also about the healthy and safe development of children
No effective prevention policy or system can be developed or implemented in isolation
Prevention science has improved, but gaps remain — much research still comes from high-income nations

lessons.title: Evidence-Based Prevention Across the Life Course
lessons.main:
Family: parenting skills programmes — strongest evidence in early and middle childhood (e.g., Strong Families-type programmes)
School: early childhood education for disadvantaged children; personal and social skills education; classroom management; school policies on substances
Community: community multi-component initiatives; media campaigns only when carefully designed; entertainment venue and workplace policies
Interventions are matched to age (prenatal to adulthood) and risk level (universal, selective, indicated)
Source: UNODC International Standards on Drug Use Prevention

lessons.title: School-Based Education: What Works
lessons.main:
Merely highlighting dangers (scare tactics) is not effective

Better results when drug education is delivered by the usual teacher — not strangers (police, doctors, ‘recovered users’)
Avoid sensational or exaggerated material
Integrate content into the usual curriculum; provide multiple short sessions
Frame realistic drug education as part of broader life education
Mass campaigns are often too simplistic relative to community expectations of what they can achieve

lessons.title: Treatment as Demand Reduction (Preview of Module 6)
lessons.main:
Detoxification and stabilization
Psychosocial counselling and rehabilitation
Therapeutic community programmes
Medically assisted treatment — drug substitution therapy
Social reintegration, community development and vocational education

Knowledge Check

Your LGA plans a one-day rally where police officers warn students about drugs with graphic images. Based on evidence, this approach will most likely:
A. Produce lasting behaviour change
B. Have little or no lasting effect — and may backfire
C. Reduce drug supply
D. Qualify as harm reduction

Answer: B — Scare tactics and outsider-delivered one-off sessions show poor outcomes.

lessons.title: What Is Harm Reduction?
lessons.main:
Policies, programmes, services and actions that reduce the health, social and economic harms of drug use to individuals, communities and society
Complements approaches that seek to prevent or reduce overall drug consumption
Often serves as a bridge to drug dependence treatment or cessation — but those are not the only goals

An important aim: keep people who use drugs alive, healthy and productive

lessons.title: Harm Reduction: A Practical, Everyday Logic
lessons.main:
Harm reduction is an old public health concept used in many areas of life
Example: compulsory motorbike helmets
Helmets do not prevent accidents — but when accidents occur, they reduce death and injury
Helmet laws do not condone bad driving; they accept that accidents happen and reduce their consequences
Helmets complement other efforts: driver education, better roads, law enforcement

lessons.title: Rationale for Harm Reduction
lessons.main:
Prevents spread of blood-borne viruses among PWID and the wider community — strong evidence that NSPs significantly reduce HIV
Gives people awareness and skills to make informed choices
Recognizes that despite education, some individuals will continue to use drugs
People should not be denied services because they engage in high-risk behaviour — the RIGHT TO HEALTH
UN commitment: 2001 Declaration of Commitment on HIV/AIDS; 2006 General Assembly Political Declaration
Country comparisons show far lower HIV among PWID where harm reduction was scaled up; at least six African countries have adopted NSP and methadone
Source: Global Commission on Drug Policy 2011

lessons.title: The Comprehensive Package: Ten Essential Interventions
lessons.main:
1. Needle and syringe programmes (NSP)
2. Opioid substitution therapy (OST) and other evidence-based drug dependence treatment
3. HIV testing and counselling
4. Antiretroviral therapy
5. Prevention and treatment of sexually transmitted infections
6. Condom programmes for PWID and their sexual partners
7. Targeted information, education and communication for PWID and partners
8. Prevention, vaccination, diagnosis and treatment of viral hepatitis
9. Prevention, diagnosis and treatment of tuberculosis
10. Naloxone for prevention and treatment of opioid overdose
Source: WHO, UNODC, UNAIDS

lessons.title: Forum Activity
lessons.main:
Group 1 question: What changes could make hospital-based drug treatment programmes accessible to more drug users?
Group 2 question: Harm reduction is not fully national policy in Nigeria — what are the key lessons about this intervention for people who use drugs?
Post your response to ONE question in the Module 3 forum and reply to a colleague who answered the other question

lessons.title: Two Cities, Two HIV Curves
lessons.main:
City A introduced needle and syringe programmes and OST early; HIV prevalence among PWID stayed low. City B prohibited both; HIV among PWID climbed sharply over the same decade.
A state assembly member asks you: “Doesn't giving out needles just encourage injecting?” You have five minutes to respond using the evidence in this module.

Discuss / respond in the LMS forum:

Summarize the strongest two evidence points you would present.
Use the helmet analogy to answer the member's question directly.
Which elements of the ten-intervention package could realistically be linked to existing KADSAMHSA and PHC services?
What outcome indicators would you propose to track?

lessons.main:

2. Effective school prevention: usual teachers, multiple integrated sessions, no scare tactics
3. Harm reduction reduces the harms of drug use without requiring abstinence first — like helmet laws

lessons.title: Drugs and Effects and Understanding Drug Dependency
lessons.main:
Online self-paced module with pre-test, knowledge checks, case study and post-test
Adapted for online delivery by KADSAMHSA from the UNODC/European Union Trainer Resource Modules, “Response to Drugs and Related Organised Crime in Nigeria” (May 2019).

lessons.title: Learning Objectives
lessons.main:
By the end of this module, you will be able to:
1. Define what a drug is and how psychoactive substances affect the central nervous system
2. Distinguish between drug use, misuse and dependence
3. Describe the drug dependence syndrome as a complex, relapsing medical condition
4. Classify drugs as depressants, stimulants and hallucinogens, with common Nigerian examples
5. Identify and correct common myths about drug dependency

Pre-Test — Check Your Starting Point (not graded)

Q1. A drug is best defined as:
A. Only an illegal substance
B. A substance (legal or illegal) that acts on the central nervous system, altering thinking, feeling and behaviour
C. Only injectable substances
D. Any food supplement
Q2. Of the ~275 million people who used illicit drugs in 2016, roughly how many had problematic use?
A. All of them
B. About 31 million
C. About 200 million
D. Fewer than 1 million
Q3. Drug dependence is best understood as:
A. A moral failure
B. A lack of willpower
C. A complex, often relapsing medical condition with biological, psychological and social components
D. A choice made daily
Q4. Drugs that slow down the central nervous system are called:
A. Stimulants
B. Depressants
C. Hallucinogens
D. Antibiotics
Q5. Which statement about cannabis is supported by this course?
A. Everyone who tries it becomes dependent
B. About one in ten users can become dependent
C. It is a stimulant
D. It has no psychoactive ingredient

lessons.title: What Is a Drug and How Does It Affect Us?
lessons.main:
A substance — legal or illegal — taken into the body that affects the central nervous system by acting on the brain and spinal cord
Alters the way a person thinks, feels and behaves
Affects the normal functioning of the body and/or brain
May also prevent or cure disease or enhance physical or mental welfare (medicines)
Routes of use: ingesting, smoking, injecting, inhaling

lessons.title: Not All Drug Use Is the Same
lessons.main:
The majority of people who use drugs do not have drug problems or dependency
Use: taking a legal or illegal drug without negative consequences — social events, recreation, experimentation, cultural or religious practice
Misuse: losing control on an occasion, causing harm to self or others (e.g., drink-driving crash) — without being dependent
‘Use’ and ‘misuse’ are preferred over ‘abuse’ — they are non-judgmental and less stigmatizing

31m

of ~275 million people who used illicit drugs in 2016 had problematic use

lessons.title: The Drug Dependence Syndrome
lessons.main:
A cluster of physiological, behavioural and cognitive experiences
Substance use takes on a much higher priority than behaviours that once had greater value
Desire — often strong, sometimes overpowering — to take the substance
Inability to control the impulse to use despite negative consequences
Physical changes in brain areas critical for judgment, decision-making, learning, memory and behaviour control
After a period of abstinence, return to use can lead to rapid reappearance of the syndrome (relapse risk)
Source: WHO ICD-10

lessons.title: How Dependence Develops: Initiation to Disorder
lessons.main:
Susceptible individuals: genetic disposition, child abuse history, psychiatric conditions, substance use in the home, social isolation
Even small exposure to a substance can alter brain chemistry; pathways are modified with repeated use
Environment shapes the path: poverty, social change, cultural norms, drug policy, availability and peer culture
Social support and integration are protective
The range runs from casual, non-problematic (even beneficial, e.g., prescribed) use to chronic dependence

lessons.title: Dependency Is a Medical Condition — Not a Moral Failure
lessons.main:
Dependence is not the result of a lack of willpower or moral weakness

It has biological, psychological and sociological components
WHO and international bodies agree: a complex, often relapsing medical condition
This framing determines the right response: treatment and care, not blame

lessons.title: What Determines a Drug's Effects?
lessons.main:
Size, weight and health of the person
Tolerance — whether the person is used to taking it
Poly-drug use — other drugs taken around the same time
The amount taken and the strength/purity of the drug (varies with illegally produced drugs)
Route of use: smoked, injected, ingested
Environment and mood — the setting and reason for taking

lessons.title: Classifying Psychoactive Drugs
lessons.main:
By effect on the central nervous system:
Depressants — slow down the CNS
Stimulants — speed up the CNS
Hallucinogens — distort the CNS
By legal status:
Over-the-counter with minimal restrictions
Restricted to medical prescription
Restricted by social policy
Completely illegal
The same drug can be freely available in one country and prescription-only in another

lessons.title: Depressants: Opioids and Heroin
lessons.main:
Opioid family: opium, codeine, morphine, heroin, pethidine, methadone, tramadol
Heroin: narcotic analgesic from the opium poppy; Nigerian street names include ‘Gabji’ and ‘Market’
Forms: white powder, tan granular form, heroin base; effects last three to six hours
Routes: injected, smoked, snorted, mixed with cannabis/tobacco
Not everyone who tries heroin becomes dependent — but physical dependence and withdrawal deter many from stopping
Major risk: overdose depressing the respiratory system — risk rises when combined with alcohol or sedatives

lessons.title: Depressant: Cannabis
lessons.main:
From the plant cannabis sativa; psychoactive ingredient THC produces the ‘high’
Forms: marijuana, hashish, hash oil; commonly smoked, eaten, or brewed as tea in Nigeria
About one in ten users can become dependent
Nigerian names: Weewee, Igbo, Weed, Kush, Skunk, Ghanja, Taba and many others
Short-term effects: loss of inhibition, altered senses and memory, anxiety/mild paranoia, reduced coordination, bloodshot eyes

lessons.title: Stimulants: Cocaine and Amphetamine-Type Stimulants
lessons.main:
Cocaine: from coca leaves; powder, freebase and crack forms; snorted, injected or smoked; names include Coke, Powder, Thailand White
Cocaine short-term: confidence, energy, alertness; long-term: insomnia, nasal damage, anxiety, paranoia, psychosis, depression
Amphetamines: stimulate the CNS like adrenaline; powder, tablet, capsule or liquid
Self-medication with amphetamine occurs among truck drivers, students, fishermen and businessmen to stave off fatigue
Inhalants (also widely misused by street-involved youth): initial euphoria then drowsiness; chronic use damages brain, liver and kidneys and can be fatal

Knowledge Check

A client uses tramadol daily, has tried to stop repeatedly, and continues despite job loss and family conflict. This pattern best matches:
A. Recreational use
B. Experimental use
C. The dependence syndrome
D. Therapeutic use

Answer: C — Loss of control, salience and continued use despite consequences are core ICD-10 dependence features.

lessons.title: True or False? Common Myths About Drug Dependency
lessons.main:
‘People dependent on drugs can stop whenever they wish’ — FALSE
‘Drug dependency is a moral failure or willpower problem’ — FALSE
‘All people who use drugs are drug dependent’ — FALSE
‘You cannot be dependent on prescribed medication’ — FALSE
‘If you can go to work, you are not really dependent’ — FALSE
‘A relapse equals failure’ / ‘Rehab doesn't work’ — FALSE: relapse is part of a chronic condition; treatment works

lessons.title: Film Activity: ‘Glue Made Me A Ghost’ (8 minutes)
lessons.main:
Watch the short film linked in the LMS — written and performed by ex-street children in Cambodia, most formerly dependent on glue
Based on real experiences: scavenging, sleeping on the streets, injuries, gang violence and the risks of inhalant use
Forum prompt: Which risk factors from the Introductory Module do you see in the children's stories? What parallels exist for street-involved children in Nigerian cities?

lessons.title: Same Drug, Different Stories
lessons.main:
Three people use codeine cough syrup: (1) a nurse takes it as prescribed after surgery for ten days; (2) a student takes large doses at parties most weekends and recently blacked out; (3) a mechanic has used it daily for two years, needs more to feel normal, and has sold tools to buy it.
A community volunteer says all three are ‘addicts’ who should be reported to the police.

Discuss / respond in the LMS forum:

Classify each person's pattern: use, misuse or dependence — and justify each classification.
What response is appropriate for each of the three?
Why is the volunteer's blanket label both inaccurate and harmful?
Which brain- and behaviour-based features would you check for in person 3?

lessons.title: Causes of Drug Use and Associated Stigma of Drug Users
lessons.main:
Online self-paced module with pre-test, knowledge checks, case study and post-test
Adapted for online delivery by KADSAMHSA from the UNODC/European Union Trainer Resource Modules, “Response to Drugs and Related Organised Crime in Nigeria” (May 2019).

lessons.title: Learning Objectives
lessons.main:
By the end of this module, you will be able to:
1. Explain that there is no single theory of why people use drugs
2. Describe the categories of drug use from experimental to dependent and therapeutic
3. Identify the social, economic and political determinants of vulnerability to drug use
4. Define stigma and describe its consequences for drug users and their families
5. Apply non-stigmatizing language and identify practical ways to reduce stigma

Pre-Test — Check Your Starting Point (not graded)

Q1. Why do people use drugs?
A. One single cause explains all drug use
B. There is no single theory — reasons are wide-ranging and multi-factorial
C. Only peer pressure
D. Only poverty
Q2. A person who tries a substance once or twice out of curiosity and stops is showing:
A. Dependent use
B. Experimental use
C. Intensive use
D. Therapeutic use
Q3. Evidence on the ‘gateway’ idea shows that:
A. Cannabis use inevitably leads to heroin
B. There is no evidence that using one drug necessarily leads people to other drugs
C. All drug users progress to injecting
D. Alcohol always precedes cannabis
Q4. Stigma is best defined as:
A. A medical diagnosis
B. A ‘stain’ marking someone as unacceptable, leading to prejudice and discrimination
C. A form of treatment
D. A legal penalty
Q5. One major consequence of stigma is that it:
A. Speeds up treatment entry
B. Delays drug users and families from seeking help
C. Reduces drug prices
D. Improves media reporting

lessons.title: Why Do People Take Drugs?
lessons.main:
There is no single theory or explanation

Despite widespread negative feelings toward drug use — and abundant information about consequences — millions start or continue
Common reasons named by communities: confidence, peer pressure, rebellion, relaxation, experimentation, curiosity, fun, loneliness, boredom, ritual, mental health, social pressures
Forum warm-up: before continuing, post three reasons you have observed in your own community

lessons.title: Ritual, Cultural and Religious Use
lessons.main:
In several societies drug use is tied to long-standing ritual, religious or cultural practice
Example: the coca leaf — chewed and brewed for centuries in the Andes; an energizer and remedy, integral to cultural tradition
Yet the leaf is often treated as equivalent to cocaine or heroin
Understanding context prevents misjudging culturally embedded practices

lessons.title: Coping With Problems and Difficulties
lessons.main:
To be accepted by peers
To deal with life's problems and bad moods
Boredom and lack of opportunity
To deal with mental health problems (self-medication)
To deal with physical pain

lessons.title: Categories of Drug Use
lessons.main:
Experimental: tried once or twice out of curiosity; not continued
Recreational: chosen for enjoyment, to enhance a mood or social occasion
Situational: used for a specific purpose or setting (e.g., staying awake to work or study)
Intensive: heavy, frequent use — escalating risk
Dependent: the dependence syndrome (Module 4)
Therapeutic: prescribed medical use

lessons.title: Why Do People Choose Certain Drugs?
lessons.main:
Effects: matched to occasion — amphetamines for energy, alcohol against stress
Availability: greater supply, more use — where cannabis is grown locally, use is more widespread
Affordability: widely available drugs tend to be cheaper
Accessibility: easy access increases use of specific drugs
Poly-drug use: mixing for a more intense experience

No evidence that using one drug necessarily leads to ‘harder’ drugs over time

lessons.title: Vulnerability: Social, Economic and Political Determinants
lessons.main:
Individual: genetics, mental health, trauma history
Family: neglect, abuse, substance use in the home
Community and society: laws and norms favourable to drug use, availability, poverty, marginalization, lack of opportunity
Vulnerability is layered — which is why single-cause explanations and single-sector responses fail
Source: UNODC 2015

Knowledge Check

Cannabis use is highest where it is grown locally and cheap. Which drivers of drug choice does this illustrate?
A. Effects and ritual
B. Availability, affordability and accessibility
C. Gateway progression
D. Peer pressure only

Answer: B

lessons.title: Self-Check: The Stigma Mirror (Part One)
lessons.main:
Answer honestly for yourself before continuing:
Your son announces he will marry someone who once received drug treatment — what is your reaction?
Would you invite a former drug user to your house for dinner?
Would you employ a former drug user in your home or organization?
Would you rent your guest room to someone once treated for a drug problem?

lessons.title: The Stigma Mirror (Part Two)
lessons.main:
Now imagine the drug user is your own son or daughter:
Would you want him or her to get married?
Would you want him or her to have a house of their own?
Would you want him or her to get a job and be self-sufficient?
Notice the shift: closeness produces compassion. Stigma shrinks when the person becomes real to us

lessons.title: What Is Stigma and What Does It Do?
lessons.main:
Stigma: a ‘stain’ marking someone as unacceptable — it leads to prejudice and discrimination
Delays help-seeking: users deny problems to avoid the ‘hopeless addict’ label; families hide the issue out of shame
Contributes to low self-esteem; builds on and reinforces existing prejudice and social inequality
Media language matters: ‘junkie’ and ‘addict’ are socially accepted but derogatory, dehumanizing terms
UK survey (3,000 respondents): far less empathy toward drug users than toward people with mental health problems — high blame and intolerance
Mental health stigma declined through sensitization — the same change is possible for drug use

lessons.title: Reducing Stigma in Practice
lessons.main:
Use person-first, neutral language: ‘person who uses drugs’, ‘person with a substance use disorder’
Present drug dependence as the medical condition it is
Engage media, religious and community leaders with accurate information
Make services welcoming and confidential — stigma at the clinic door defeats every other investment
Model the change: staff and volunteers audit their own language and assumptions

lessons.title: The Radio Phone-In
lessons.main:
A popular Kaduna radio host runs a phone-in titled ‘Ridding our streets of junkies’. Callers demand arrests and public shaming. The host invites KADSAMHSA to send a guest ‘to defend the addicts’.
You are the guest. You have one 10-minute segment and two caller questions to change the frame of the conversation.

Discuss / respond in the LMS forum:

What alternative title/frame would you propose to the producer, and why does language matter?
Which two evidence points from Modules 4–5 would you use on air?
How would you answer a caller who says stigma is ‘useful because it discourages drug use’?
What single call-to-action would you leave listeners with?

lessons.title: Types of Drug Treatment

lessons.title: Learning Objectives
lessons.main:
By the end of this module, you will be able to:
1. Describe the global and African treatment gap and the aims of drug treatment
2. State the principles of effective treatment
3. Describe the main treatment modalities: counselling, detoxification, residential, outpatient/community-based, mutual help, and substitution therapy
4. Explain the benefits and limits of each modality and who each suits best
5. Relate treatment barriers in Nigeria to service design at state level

Pre-Test — Check Your Starting Point (not graded)

Q1. Globally, about how many people who need drug treatment can access it?
A. 1 in 2
B. 1 in 6
C. All
D. 1 in 100
Q2. Detoxification on its own is:
A. Complete treatment
B. Not treatment — it must be followed by behavioural therapy and/or medication
C. Only for alcohol
D. Illegal
Q3. The main substitution medicines for opioid dependence are:
A. Aspirin and paracetamol
B. Methadone and buprenorphine
C. Diazepam and codeine
D. There are none
Q4. Which principle of effective treatment is correct?
A. A single treatment works for everyone
B. Treatment must address multiple needs of the person, not just drug use
C. Short treatment is always sufficient
D. Plans should never change
Q5. Residential treatment outcomes are generally better with stays of at least:
A. Three days
B. Three weeks
C. Three months
D. Three years

lessons.title: The Treatment Gap
lessons.main:
Demand for treatment keeps rising; supply of services does not
Beds and services are unavailable, or priced beyond most of the population

Closing this gap is a central task for agencies like KADSAMHSA

1 in 18

people in Africa who need drug treatment can access it — globally the figure is 1 in 6
Source: National Institute on Drug Abuse 2012

lessons.title: What Treatment Aims To Do
lessons.main:
Improve the health and quality of life of people with drug dependence
Work toward abstinence and reduce injury and death associated with high-risk use
Major interventions: counselling, detoxification, abstinence-based residential and outpatient care, mutual help groups, drug substitution programmes
Remember: drug dependence is a chronic, relapsing medical condition — treatment is managed accordingly

lessons.title: Principles of Effective Treatment
lessons.main:
No single treatment is appropriate for everyone
Treatment needs to be readily available
Attend to the multiple needs of the individual — not just the drug use
Remaining in treatment for an adequate period is critical
Continually assess and adjust the treatment plan as the person's needs change

lessons.title: Counselling
lessons.main:
An interactive, confidential exchange helping clients explore problems and build capacity to solve them
A trained counsellor collects relevant information and offers professional guidance in a formal setting
Formats: individual, couples, small groups, family or support people
Most effective when voluntary — engagement and empowerment matter
Counselling is a learned skill, not a conversation; motivational interviewing is an evidence-based approach
The counsellor never simply tells the person what to do
On its own counselling will not resolve every drug problem — links to other treatment services are essential

lessons.title: Detoxification (Withdrawal Management)
lessons.main:
Allows the body to rid itself of a drug while managing withdrawal symptoms; usually 7–14 days
Often the first step — must be followed by behavioural therapy and/or medication

Detoxification alone, with no follow-up, is not treatment

Primary goal is patient safety, not long-term abstinence; never withhold detox over doubts about commitment
Supportive care and patient choice are crucial; plan post-withdrawal care from the start

lessons.title: Residential Treatment
lessons.main:
Hospital or non-hospital settings; three-month stays produce better outcomes; therapeutic communities run 6–12 months
Focus: ‘un-learning’ harmful behaviours; building skills and attitudes for a drug-free life; personal responsibility
Highly structured activities examine damaging beliefs and destructive patterns
Limits: high drop-out; expensive; does not suit everyone; aftercare essential to prevent relapse
In many low/middle-income countries, some centres offer poor services, untrained staff and prison-like conditions — relapse after release is common

lessons.title: Outpatient and Community-Based Treatment
lessons.main:
Located in the community; mobilizes community resources; psychosocial approach; continuum of care linked to health and social services
Suits people in stable, supportive environments or without funds for residential care; same principles, lower cost
Model components:
CSOs identify users, screen and refer to primary health services
Health centres provide screening, counselling, primary care and referral to hospitals for specialized care
Welfare agencies and NGOs add education, vocational training, income generation and psychosocial support

This is the logic behind KADSAMHSA's PHC-level integration of care

lessons.title: Mutual Help Groups and Substitution Therapy
lessons.main:
Mutual help: 12-step model (AA/NA principles); complements and extends professional treatment; social support for abstinence during and after treatment
Substitution: replacing a drug with a medically prescribed one — available for nicotine, alcohol and opioids
No suitable substitutes yet for cocaine, ATS or cannabis
For opioid dependence: methadone or buprenorphine — both WHO essential medicines; no ‘high’, markedly reduced craving
Benefits: better health and social functioning, reduced crime, mortality and blood-borne virus transmission; relatively inexpensive; 12-month duration produces better outcomes; can lead to full abstinence

Knowledge Check

A client completes 10 days of inpatient detox and is discharged with no follow-up plan. According to this module, the service has provided:
A. Complete treatment
B. Withdrawal management only — not treatment
C. Substitution therapy
D. A therapeutic community programme

Answer: B

lessons.title: Treatment Barriers in Nigeria — and What They Imply
lessons.main:
Barriers (Module 1): prohibitive cost, fear and stigma, unavailability, no information on where to find help
Service design responses:
Decentralize: bring screening and basic care to PHC level
Reduce cost: subsidized or insured care (e.g., behavioral health coverage initiatives)
Reduce stigma: confidential, welcoming, person-first services
Inform: publicize referral pathways and entry points

lessons.title: Forum Activity: Counselling Questions
lessons.main:
Choose ONE and post your answer in the Module 6 forum:
1. Why do you think drug users do not seek counselling?
2. Why must counselling be voluntary (outside treatment-centre settings)?
3. From your experience, why is maintaining confidentiality so important in drug treatment counselling?
Reply to at least one colleague who answered a different question

lessons.title: Matching the Client to the Modality
lessons.main:
Four clients present at a KADSAMHSA-supported centre: (A) a 32-year-old trader, opioid-dependent for 6 years, two failed detox attempts, stable family; (B) a 19-year-old student using cannabis heavily for 8 months, supportive parents; (C) a 40-year-old man, severe poly-drug dependence, homeless, chaotic environment; (D) a 28-year-old woman who completed residential treatment last month.
Resources available: outpatient counselling, a 16-week structured programme, residential beds, peer support groups, and (hypothetically) an OST pilot.

Discuss / respond in the LMS forum:

Match each client to the most appropriate primary modality and justify using module principles.
For client A, why might counselling alone fail? What does the evidence suggest?
For client D, what does the module say about the period after residential treatment?
Which client(s) illustrate why ‘no single treatment fits everyone’?

lessons.main:

2. No single treatment fits everyone; adequate duration and attention to multiple needs are critical
3. Detoxification alone is not treatment; it must connect to ongoing care

lessons.title: Learning Objectives
lessons.main:
By the end of this module, you will be able to:
1. Describe the specific patterns and risks of drug use among women, including in Nigeria
2. Explain why women who use drugs are a hidden population and face distinct treatment barriers
3. Summarize the health risks facing people who inject drugs, including HIV, hepatitis C, overdose and TB
4. Describe HIV trends among PWID in Nigeria and the role of the harm reduction package
5. Explain why young people (10–24) are a distinct vulnerable population

Pre-Test — Check Your Starting Point (not graded)

A. One tenth
B. One third
C. One half
D. Two thirds
Q2. Globally, women are more likely than men to misuse:

B. Prescription drugs, particularly opioids and tranquillizers
C. Inhalants
D. No substances

B. Fell from 5.6% to 3.4%
C. Stayed at 10%
D. Was never measured

A. 2%

C. 52%
D. 92%

lessons.title: Women Who Use Drugs: The Global Picture
lessons.main:
Women are more likely than men to misuse prescription drugs — particularly opioids and tranquillizers
In Nigeria: 3.4 million women reported past-year drug use (vs 10.8 million men)

Yet only one in five drug users in treatment worldwide is a woman

1 in 3

of the world's drug users is a woman; ~3.5 million women inject drugs

lessons.title: Elevated HIV Risk Among Women Who Inject
lessons.main:
HIV prevalence is generally higher among females who inject drugs (FWID) than males across regions
Drug use and sex work often overlap, creating dual risk (unsafe sex + unsafe injecting):
Asia: FWID who sell sex are ~20× more likely than other female sex workers to acquire HIV
Tanzania: 85% of FWID also sell sex; HIV 62% (vs 28% among men who inject)
Nepal: half of FWID sell sex; HIV 33% vs 6.3% among male injectors
In Nigeria: HIV among female injectors is about five times higher than male counterparts

lessons.title: Women Using Drugs in Nigeria: Survey Findings
lessons.main:
Women high-risk users more likely than men to have sex with other drug users (67% vs 46%)
Nearly half of women (vs one third of men) reported a steady partner who also used drugs
Women more likely to report a steady partner who injects (28% vs 11%)
Men were 3× more likely to pay for sex; women 4–5× more likely to receive money or drugs for sex
Arrests for sex work almost exclusively reported among women — highest among women who inject
Source: Drug Use in Nigeria 2018

lessons.title: A Hidden Population
lessons.main:
Hard to reach and under-represented in drug treatment services
High concealment of drug use due to intense stigma, societal disapproval and demonization — especially of mothers
Pathways to dependence: male injecting partners, domestic violence and intimidation, histories of sexual abuse, low self-esteem, isolation, sex work
Vulnerabilities: fear of exposure; difficulty accessing clean equipment; sharing a partner's needle; being injected by someone else
Treatment barriers: services not tailored to women; no childcare; fear of losing custody

Knowledge Check

A treatment centre reports that almost no women enrol, and concludes ‘women here don't use drugs’. What does this module suggest?
A. The conclusion is correct
B. Women who use drugs are a hidden population — low enrolment reflects concealment, stigma and service barriers, not absence of need
C. Women cannot become dependent
D. Women only use alcohol

Answer: B

lessons.title: People Who Inject Drugs: Nigeria
lessons.main:
~80,000 people estimated to have injected drugs; 1 in 5 high-risk users injects; 78% men
Women who inject were more likely to inject heroin and engage in higher-risk sexual behaviour
HIV among PWID declined: 5.6% (2007) → 4.2% (2010) → 3.4% (2014), with rising sterile-needle use over the period
IBBSS 2014: 44% of PWID knew someone who had died of AIDS
Self-reported HIV among high-risk users ~6%; among PWID ~9% (subject to reporting bias)
Source: IBBSS 2014; Drug Use in Nigeria 2018

lessons.title: Beyond HIV: The Wider Health Burden of Injecting
lessons.main:
Hepatitis C: PWID have rates 25× the general population; ~52% of PWID globally; 60–70% of chronic carriers develop chronic liver disease
Overdose: second most common cause of death among illicit drug users; ~35% of global illicit drug mortality; most deaths accidental, 1–3 hours after opioid use
TB: people with HIV who inject have 2–6× the risk of developing TB
Vein and soft-tissue injuries from repeated injecting
Compounding factors: criminalization, unfriendly services, fear of arrest, poverty, homelessness

lessons.title: The Harm Reduction Package for PWID
lessons.main:
The WHO/UNAIDS/UNODC-supported package (Module 3) directly addresses these risks: NSP, OST, testing, ART, STI care, condoms, targeted IEC, hepatitis services, TB services, naloxone
Evidence: risks fall measurably where the package is implemented at scale
Service design principle: meet women and young people where they are, with tailored, confidential entry points

lessons.title: Young People (10–24): A Time of Transition
lessons.main:
Physical, emotional and social transitions define this period
More vulnerable young people experience more: unprotected sex, STIs including HIV, unintended pregnancy, violence, mental health disorders — and substance use
Early initiation raises the risk of later problems — prevention and youth-friendly services are the priority responses
Links directly to school-based and community programming (Module 3) and to family interventions (Module 10)

lessons.title: Amina's Second Visit
lessons.main:
Amina, 26, attends a PHC for a wound on her arm. The nurse suspects injecting. Amina is evasive, mentions her partner ‘handles the injections’, has a 3-year-old child, and leaves before testing is discussed. She returns two weeks later, pregnant, and asks whether the clinic will report her to anyone.
The facility has HIV testing, antenatal care, and a referral line to a KADSAMHSA treatment centre. There is no female counsellor on duty today.

Discuss / respond in the LMS forum:

Which vulnerability factors from this module does Amina's story illustrate?
What should the nurse say to the confidentiality question — and why does the answer determine everything that follows?
Design Amina's next three service steps using the harm reduction package and women-specific considerations.
What structural changes would make this facility genuinely accessible to women who use drugs?

lessons.title: Drug Screening: Steps to Take
lessons.main:
Online self-paced module with pre-test, knowledge checks, case study and post-test
Adapted for online delivery by KADSAMHSA from the UNODC/European Union Trainer Resource Modules, “Response to Drugs and Related Organised Crime in Nigeria” (May 2019).

lessons.title: Learning Objectives
lessons.main:
By the end of this module, you will be able to:
1. Explain why drug screening matters and who can conduct it
2. Identify the groups of people who should be screened and the substances covered
3. Administer the ASSIST screening approach with rapport, sensitivity and confidentiality
4. Score ASSIST responses and interpret lower, moderate and high risk levels
5. Match risk levels to the correct response: no treatment, brief intervention, or referral

Pre-Test — Check Your Starting Point (not graded)

Q1. ASSIST stands for:
A. Alcohol, Smoking and Substance Involvement Screening Test
B. Advanced Substance Screening Instrument
C. African Standard Substance Inventory
D. Assessment of Serious Intoxication
Q2. Who can administer the ASSIST screening?
A. Only psychiatrists
B. A range of trained workers — nurses, community health workers, social workers, GPs and others in contact with people who use drugs
C. Only police officers
D. Only laboratory scientists
Q3. In ASSIST scoring, 'daily or almost daily' use in the past 3 months scores:
A. 0
B. 2
C. 4
D. 6
Q4. A 'moderate risk' ASSIST score calls for:
A. No action
B. A brief intervention
C. Immediate arrest
D. Compulsory admission
Q5. The manner of administering ASSIST matters because:
A. It changes the scoring rules
B. A friendly, non-judgmental, confidential approach improves consent and accuracy of answers
C. It is legally required to be hostile
D. Clients cannot understand questions otherwise

lessons.title: Why Screen for Substance Use?
lessons.main:
Deaths and injuries linked to drugs are a global public health burden
Drug use is linked to social, financial, legal and relationship problems
Use is not declining — and is likely to get worse without action
Screening detects harmful use early and can avert progression to dependence
Every screening is an opportunity to educate people about the risks of hazardous use

lessons.title: Who Can Screen — and Who Should Be Screened?
lessons.main:
Screeners: primary health care workers and anyone in contact with people who use drugs:
Community health workers, mental health workers, nurses
Social workers, physicians, general practitioners, psychologists
People to screen:
Anyone from young adulthood
Attendees of STI clinics, university health services and mental health settings
People with complaints suggesting drug use issues
New prisoners — particularly for drug-associated offences
People whose condition would be worsened by substance use
Pregnant women

lessons.title: Substances Covered — and Local Names Matter
lessons.main:
The range assessed is broad, including tobacco and alcohol — highly hazardous psychoactive substances
Global drug names are used, but always consider local names to avoid misinterpretation (e.g., ‘Gabji’ for heroin, ‘Weewee’/‘Igbo’ for cannabis)
The screener should know common drugs and side effects, and understand the difference between use, misuse and dependence

lessons.title: Administering ASSIST: Building Trust
lessons.main:
A person is more likely to consent and answer accurately when the health worker:
Shows they are listening; is friendly and non-judgmental
Shows sensitivity and empathy
Provides information about the screening and carefully explains why substance questions are asked
Explains confidentiality clearly
Use gentle prompts to check answers — e.g., an older client who says ‘no’ to cannabis may reconsider when asked about use at school or parties years ago

lessons.title: Scoring Responses (Past Three Months)
lessons.main:
Never — not used at all in the last 3 months → score 0
Once or twice — 1–2 times in the last 3 months → score 2
Monthly — average 1–3 times per month → score 3
Weekly — average 1–4 times per week → score 4
Daily or almost daily — 5–7 days per week → score 6
Once confirmed a person never used a drug, do not keep repeating that drug in later questions

lessons.title: Interpreting Scores and Choosing the Response
lessons.main:
Lower risk: score 3 or less (alcohol: 10 or less) → no treatment needed; brief feedback
Moderate risk → brief intervention
High risk → referral to specialist assessment and treatment

The majority of people screened will require no further assistance

Risk is modified by family history, psychiatric comorbidity, age, gender and socioeconomic status — consider these in assessing the individual

Knowledge Check

A client scores in the moderate risk band for cannabis and lower risk for all other substances. The correct next step is:
A. No action at all
B. A brief intervention focused on cannabis
C. Immediate referral to residential treatment
D. Report to law enforcement

Answer: B

lessons.title: The Brief Intervention and Motivational Interviewing
lessons.main:
Aim: help the person understand their substance use is a risk — motivating them to reduce or cease use
Motivational interviewing: directs people to explore and resolve their own doubts (the ‘good things’ vs the ‘less good things’) and move through the stages of change
Built on empathy: accepting, non-judgmental, respectful, never argumentative, avoiding labels like ‘drug addict’
Duration: from three minutes up to 15–30 minutes

lessons.title: Practice Activity One: Score the Client (LMS Quiz)
lessons.main:
In the LMS, you will read a short dialogue between a health worker and a client
Using the score table (0 / 2 / 3 / 4 / 6), assign a score for each substance mentioned
Then classify the client's overall risk band and select the matching response
Your scores are auto-checked against the answer key — review any mismatch before proceeding

lessons.title: Practice Activity Two: Score the Recorded Interview
lessons.main:
Watch the demonstration ASSIST interview video linked in the LMS
As you watch, score each of the client's answers on the downloadable scoring sheet
Pause after the final question, total your scores, and choose the risk band and matching response
Then open the model scoring in the LMS and review any item where your score differed
Optional: record yourself reading the ASSIST questions aloud and listen back — aim for a friendly, neutral, unhurried tone

lessons.title: Screening at the PHC: Ibrahim
lessons.main:
Ibrahim, 29, attends a PHC Centre of Excellence with poor sleep and stomach pain. Asked about substances, he reports: tramadol ‘most days of the week’ for the past year; cannabis about once a month; alcohol once or twice in three months; no other substances. He has tried to cut down twice, and a friend has expressed concern.
You are the trained screener on duty, with the ASSIST forms and a referral pathway to a KADSAMHSA treatment centre.

Discuss / respond in the LMS forum:

Assign frequency scores for tramadol, cannabis and alcohol using the 0/2/3/4/6 scale.
Which substance is likely to place Ibrahim in a higher risk band, and what is the matching response?
Draft the first two sentences you would say to Ibrahim when giving feedback — non-judgmental and specific.
What details go into the referral if specialist assessment is indicated?

lessons.main:

2. Rapport, empathy and clear confidentiality drive consent and accurate answers

4. Risk bands map to responses: none → brief feedback; moderate → brief intervention; high → referral
