lessons.title: Learning Objectives
lessons.main:
By the end of this module, you will be able to:
1. Define advocacy and explain why it is needed in the drug use response
2. State the principles of advocacy, including avoiding increased harm
3. Apply the eight-step advocacy planning framework
4. Identify advocacy targets and build a coalition with the right membership
5. Write SMART advocacy objectives and outline an action plan

Pre-Test — Check Your Starting Point (not graded)

Q1. Advocacy is best described as:
A. Providing clinical treatment
B. Influencing decision-making to develop, establish or change policies, programmes and services
C. Fundraising only
D. Arresting offenders
Q2. A core principle of advocacy in this field is that activities should:
A. Maximize publicity at any cost
B. Avoid increasing harm to drug users
C. Exclude drug users from planning
D. Ignore evidence
Q3. SMART objectives are:
A. Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-constrained
B. Simple, Modern, Ambitious, Rapid, Total
C. Strategic, Military, Active, Regional, Tough
D. None of these
Q4. The first step of the advocacy planning framework is to:
A. Create an action plan
B. Select an issue or problem to address
C. Identify allies
D. Monitor and evaluate
Q5. 'Support Don't Punish' is:
A. A treatment medication
B. An international advocacy campaign questioning punitive drug policy
C. A police unit
D. A UN convention

lessons.title: What Is Advocacy?
lessons.main:
“Advocacy aims at influencing decision-making, with the goals of developing, establishing or changing policies and establishing and sustaining programmes and services” — WHO (2003)
Action directed at changing the policies, positions or programmes of any institution
An ongoing process to change values, attitudes, actions, policies and laws by influencing decision-makers, opinion leaders, organizations and systems at different levels

lessons.title: Why Advocacy Is Needed
lessons.main:
Widespread criminalization leaves many drug users marginalized, vulnerable and without needed health services
Drug users are commonly the most disliked group in any community — seen as criminals, diseased, useless
That attitude feeds stigma and discrimination — and drives resistance to effective programmes

Advocacy is how evidence gets translated into policy and services

lessons.title: Principles of Advocacy
lessons.main:
Advocacy activities should avoid increasing harm — e.g., outreach permitted only on condition police can arrest clients would harm the people it serves
Balance short-term pragmatic goals with long-term developmental goals
Objectives relate to approaches shown by research to be effective
Activities are specific, targeted, and fit the social, cultural and political context of society

lessons.title: The Eight-Step Advocacy Planning Framework
lessons.main:
Step 1: Select an issue or problem you want to address
Step 2: Analyze and research the issue
Step 3: Develop specific objectives for your advocacy work
Step 4: Identify your targets
Step 5: Identify your allies
Step 6: Identify your resources
Step 7: Create an action plan
Step 8: Implement, monitor and evaluate

lessons.title: Targets and Allies
lessons.main:
Typical targets: politicians, health bureaucrats, law enforcement (including corrections), mainstream health workers, media, religious leaders, community leaders, neighbours of programmes
Coalition membership: start small, grow with needed skills:
Doctors, health and social workers, lawyers
Drug users themselves — their insights directly affect their community
Harm reduction practitioners, nurses, NGO staff
Media representatives

lessons.title: Are Your Objectives Achievable? Ask First
lessons.main:
Is the issue so sensitive that policymakers cannot be approached directly?
Have others tried advocating on this issue — what lessons did they learn?
Is sufficient information available to persuade policymakers? If not, the objective should include collecting it

lessons.title: Make Objectives SMART
lessons.main:
Specific — states clearly what the programme aims to achieve
Measurable — measurable without massive resources
Achievable — pragmatic, within available finance and staff
Relevant — useful to the process of working toward the goal
Time-constrained — met within the set timeframe

Knowledge Check

‘We will improve public attitudes to drug users’ fails as a SMART objective mainly because it is:
A. Too specific
B. Not measurable or time-constrained
C. Too short
D. Illegal

Answer: B

lessons.title: Action Plans: General Tips
lessons.main:
For each objective and audience, deliver consistent messages, through a variety of media, from a variety of sources, over an extended period
Plan events with credible spokespersons from coalition partners
Delegate responsibilities clearly for implementing and monitoring specific activities
Organize training and practice in advocacy
Identify, verify and incorporate key facts and data to support objectives

lessons.title: Case in Point: Support Don't Punish
lessons.main:
An international campaign questioning punitive approaches to drug use
Day of Action 2013: events in 41 cities across 20 countries — the simple message caught the public imagination
“I believe drugs have destroyed many people, but wrong government policies have destroyed many more.” — Kofi Annan, former UN Secretary-General
Lesson: a clear message, broad coalition and repeated delivery can shift the debate

lessons.title: Forum Activity
lessons.main:
Post your answer to ONE question in the Module 9 forum:
1. What are the main opportunities and advantages of undertaking advocacy on drug use in your community?
2. What are the main challenges to undertaking advocacy on drug use in your community?
Reply to a colleague who answered the other question

lessons.title: A Mini Advocacy Plan for Kaduna
lessons.main:
Your coalition wants LGA chairpersons to publicly endorse referral (rather than arrest) for minor possession cases involving young people, in line with alternatives-to-incarceration practice directions.
You have: survey data on treatment barriers, two supportive religious leaders, a sympathetic radio producer, and a small budget for one quarter.

Discuss / respond in the LMS forum:

Work through steps 1–4 of the planning framework for this issue in bullet form.
Write ONE SMART objective for the quarter.
Who are your three highest-value targets and what message fits each?
What could go wrong that would increase harm — and how do you guard against it?

lessons.title: Interventions and Responses to Drug Problems in the Family
lessons.main:

Adapted for online delivery by KADSAMHSA from the UNODC/European Union Trainer Resource Modules, “Response to Drugs and Related Organised Crime in Nigeria” (May 2019).

lessons.title: Learning Objectives
lessons.main:
By the end of this module, you will be able to:
1. Describe the ripple effect of drug use from the individual to family and society
2. Summarize how family members are affected by a relative's drug use
3. Identify the three ways adult family members' support helps their drug-using relative
4. Describe the 5-Step Method and the evidence for its effectiveness
5. Apply the social network diagram to map support around an affected family member

Pre-Test — Check Your Starting Point (not graded)

Q1. The 'ripple effect' of drug use refers to:
A. Effects only on the user
B. Impacts spreading from the individual to family, friends and wider society
C. Water contamination
D. Price fluctuations
Q2. Compared to others, family members of drug users experience:
A. Lower healthcare use
B. Higher levels of depression, anxiety, somatic complaints and healthcare costs
C. No measurable effects
D. Guaranteed immunity to stress
Q3. The 5-Step Method focuses primarily on:
A. The drug user only
B. Affected and concerned family members
C. Law enforcement
D. Schools
Q4. In Step 3 of the 5-Step Method, the three broad coping positions are:
A. Engage, tolerate, withdraw
B. Fight, flight, freeze
C. Deny, accept, report
D. None of these
Q5. Evidence from the UK and Italy shows the 5-Step Method:
A. Has no effect
B. Significantly reduces psychological and physical symptoms in family members and improves coping
C. Only works for alcohol
D. Worsens family stress

lessons.title: The Ripple Effect
lessons.main:
Drug use is often treated as a ‘private’ act of an individual — but its consequences never stay private
Impacts move outward: individual → family → friends → community → society
Community-level effects include robberies, violence and insecurity — the public becomes a victim too
In Nigeria's large family structures, each user's drug problem touches many more people than in small-family societies

lessons.title: How Family Members Are Affected
lessons.main:
Higher levels of depression, anxiety and somatic complaints
More frequent use of health services and higher total healthcare costs
High rates of marital separation and divorce; low marital satisfaction
Increased interpersonal conflicts, financial strain and exposure to violence
Children of drug users often experience difficult childhoods

lessons.title: Families Are Rarely the Focus of Services
lessons.main:
Service delivery traditionally focuses on the drug user; attention to the family is occasional, less intense, shorter
Three broad categories of family-involved responses exist:
Working with families to get the user into treatment — e.g., CRAFT (Community Reinforcement and Family Training)
Involving families in the user's treatment itself
Responding to the family members' own needs in their own right
Family support helps in three ways: influencing the course of the problem; improving the relative's outcomes and treatment engagement; and reducing harm to other family members

lessons.title: The 5-Step Method: Principles
lessons.main:
Focused on affected and concerned family members — in their own right

Family members are viewed as ordinary people responding to highly stressful experiences — not as causes of the problem
Flexible and adaptable to a range of settings and circumstances
The person delivering it matters and needs training — professional primary healthcare workers are suitable
Evidence from the UK and Italy shows it is a very promising approach to reducing family-related harm

lessons.title: Steps 1 and 2: Listen, Reassure, Inform
lessons.main:
Step 1 — Listen and reassure: establish what life is like for the family member; set boundaries and goals; agree how future contact happens; follow up missed appointments. For some families, Step 1 is all that is required
Step 2 — Provide relevant, specific, targeted information:
Share evidence and facts about specific drugs, potential harms and dependence
Balance too little information (raises concern) against too much (creates confusion)
Provide written and verbal explanations; share contacts of other helpful agencies

lessons.title: Step 3: Explore Coping Responses
lessons.main:
Identify the family's current coping position:
ENGAGE — standing up to the problem
TOLERATE — putting up with it (associated with ill-health; puts the user's needs before the family's)
WITHDRAW — becoming independent of the problem
Explore advantages and disadvantages of the current response, then of alternatives

Stay alert to the risk of domestic violence and work to minimize it

lessons.title: Steps 4 and 5: Support Networks and Further Help
lessons.main:
Step 4 — Explore social support: map family, friends and agencies on a social network diagram (+ supportive, − non-supportive, +/− mixed, 0 neutral); maximize positives, neutralize negatives
Step 5 — Discuss further needs and referral:
Further help for the family member; help for the user
Sessions for the whole family or other members
Onward referral to other agencies

Key aim: consolidate the work and promote hope that the situation can improve

Knowledge Check

A mother says she pays her son's drug debts and hides his use from his father 'to keep peace'. In 5-Step terms, this coping position is:
A. Engaging
B. Tolerating — associated with ill health and putting the user's needs first
C. Withdrawing
D. Referring

Answer: B

lessons.title: What the Evidence Shows
lessons.main:
Significant reductions in psychological and physical symptoms among family members
Significant improvement in coping
Significant positive change in attitudes of the primary care professionals delivering it
Positive effects extend to the substance user as well

lessons.title: Three Families, Three Responses (Forum Activity)
lessons.main:
Scenario A: A husband discovers his wife has a serious drinking problem — draw and explain a social network diagram of his available support.
Scenario B: A wife confirms her husband is using drugs and behaving erratically; she is desperately seeking help for herself — describe the services she would want.
Scenario C: You are establishing a service for family members of people with alcohol and drug problems — anticipate the key challenges you will face.

For A: label each person/agency +, −, +/− or 0 and name your characters.
For B: which of the 5 Steps address her needs, and in what order?
For C: how will you reach families who hide the problem out of shame?

lessons.title: The Development of Human Rights
lessons.main:
People have always held rights and responsibilities within family, religion, community and state
The United Nations was founded on a pledge to promote and respect human rights for all
Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR) adopted 1948 by 56 UN members; its principles now appear in most national constitutions
30 articles — from the right to equality (Art. 1) and freedom from discrimination (Art. 2) onward
Not legally binding, but widely regarded as ‘a common standard of achievement for all people and all nations’

lessons.title: What Are Human Rights?
lessons.main:
Belong to every individual, without discrimination or discretion, forever
Universal — a birthright of every member of the human family; they define what governments can, cannot and should do to us
Inalienable — one cannot and should not lose their rights
Indivisible — no one can be denied rights because someone decides they are ‘less human’ than another
ICCPR (civil/political rights) + ICESCR (economic/social/cultural rights) + UDHR = the International Bill of Human Rights

lessons.title: The Three Drug Control Conventions
lessons.main:
1961 Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs (amended 1972): opium and derivatives, coca/cocaine, cannabis
1971 Convention on Psychotropic Substances: manufactured psychoactives — amphetamines, benzodiazepines, LSD and others
1988 Convention Against Illicit Traffic: suppressing trafficking, money-laundering and precursor control; requires criminalizing possession/purchase of controlled drugs
Together they form the framework within which national drug laws — including Nigeria's — operate

lessons.title: What the Conventions Actually Say
lessons.main:
Restrict controlled drugs to medical and scientific purposes — but are not a justification for a repressive ‘prohibitionist’ model of imprisonment and severe punishment

Their adopted vision is protecting public health

They call for social cohesion and reintegration — people affected by drugs need social protection, health care and community solidarity, not punishment
They call for science-based prevention and treatment; they never mention or support compulsory treatment
They are not against harm reduction (when not isolated from demand reduction) nor against controlled medicines in treating dependence
They never support the death penalty for drug-related crimes

lessons.title: The Right to Health — and How Criminalization Undermines It
lessons.main:
ICESCR Article 12: everyone's right to the highest attainable standard of health — including people who use drugs
Criminalization drives risky practices: sharing syringes, hurried injecting in unsafe places to avoid detection
Consequences: greater risk of overdose, vascular injuries and infections (HIV, hepatitis C)
The comprehensive harm reduction package (Module 3) is endorsed by WHO, UNODC, UNAIDS and supported by UN human rights bodies

lessons.title: Liberty and Life: Where Policy Crosses the Line
lessons.main:
Arbitrary arrest and detention: police sometimes target areas near treatment services; arrest counts used as ‘success’ indicators
Large numbers held in prolonged pre-trial detention for minor drug offences; incarceration rates of 50–90% among people who use drugs, with elevated health risks in prison
Right to life: death sentences are restricted to the ‘most serious crimes’; the INCB says the death penalty should be abolished for drug offences
Yet 33 countries/territories retain it for drugs; an estimated 600–1,000 drug-related executions annually

lessons.title: Coercive and Compulsory 'Treatment'
lessons.main:
People are frequently detained for ‘treatment’ on police suspicion or a urine test — coercive treatment becomes a form of incarceration
Compulsory detention centres subject detainees to strenuous forced exercise, beatings, solitary confinement and forced labour
Practices are not evidence-based; informed consent is disregarded; abuse, including sexual violence, is reported
The UN has called for closure of compulsory centres — yet approximately 235,000 people remain detained in East and South-East Asia alone

lessons.title: Women, Children and Generalized Discrimination
lessons.main:
Women are imprisoned for drug offences more than for any other crime — closely linked to poverty and disempowerment
Women who use drugs risk losing custody, forced sterilization or abortion, penalties for use during pregnancy, and violence — including from partners and law enforcement
Children who use drugs face criminal prosecution, often with no access to harm reduction or treatment
A drug conviction record obstructs employment, custody, benefits and travel
“A criminal record for a young person for a minor drug offence can be a far greater threat to their well-being than occasional drug use.” — Kofi Annan (2015)

Knowledge Check

A commentator claims 'the UN conventions require harsh imprisonment of drug users.' Based on this module, this claim is:
A. Accurate
B. Inaccurate — the conventions' vision is public health, reintegration and proportionate, science-based responses
C. Accurate for cannabis only
D. Impossible to assess

Answer: B

lessons.title: The Nigerian Context
lessons.main:
NDLEA Act 1989 (amended 2004): 15–25 years' imprisonment for unlawful possession or use of narcotics — of whatever quantity, for whatever purpose; compulsory treatment can be ordered
International evidence: eradication-and-criminalization approaches carry unintended consequences — organized crime, violence, rights violations
A 2015 Nigerian study (95 people who use drugs across six states, communities and prisons) documented a range of abuses — rarely otherwise recorded
Reform direction: proportionate responses and health-based alternatives — e.g., alternatives-to-incarceration practice directions now operating in Kaduna State

lessons.title: Voices From the 2015 Nigeria Study
lessons.main:
From the study interviews: a drug control officer says, “Imagine a situation where you arrest offenders and you as a state commander do not have resources to feed them in your custody due to low funding. Do you expect me to feed them from my salary?” Detainees describe prolonged pre-trial detention and pressure to pay for release.
You are preparing a KADSAMHSA briefing on rights-respecting alternatives for minor possession cases, aimed at police leadership.

Discuss / respond in the LMS forum:

Which specific rights issues does the officer's statement reveal (for detainees AND for the system)?
Which convention principles support diversion to treatment over detention for minor cases?
How do alternatives-to-incarceration referral pathways address both the rights problem and the resources problem?
What two indicators would show your briefing changed practice?

2. The drug conventions' vision is public health, reintegration and science-based responses — not maximal punishment
3. Criminalization drives riskier drug use and mass detention; compulsory 'treatment' is a rights abuse
4. Women and children face distinct, severe rights violations under punitive regimes
5. Nigeria's strict statutory penalties coexist with a reform direction toward proportionate, health-based alternatives

lessons.title: Learning Objectives
lessons.main:
By the end of this module, you will be able to:
1. Summarize the Nigerian drug situation as it concerns law enforcement
2. Describe common law enforcement views on drug use and the reasons for reluctance toward public health approaches
3. Explain why law enforcement is uniquely well placed to steer people who use drugs to assistance
4. Describe the use of discretion and the range of options for dealing with drug use offenders
5. Outline how law enforcement and health services collaborate successfully

Pre-Test — Check Your Starting Point (not graded)

A. No priority
B. Equal priority
C. Priority to enforcement only
D. Priority to demand reduction only
Q2. Law enforcement is well placed to steer drug users to help because officers:

B. Are available 24/7 and meet users at 'treatable moments' of crisis

D. Control drug prices
Q3. When police actively target public health services for drug users, a documented result is:

B. Users avoid services, adopt riskier practices and move beyond providers' reach

Q4. A 'drug diversion' scheme means:

B. Weighing the gravity of the offence in deciding the response, as is done for minor assaults, theft and traffic offences

lessons.title: The Enforcement Context in Nigeria
lessons.main:
Nigeria remains a key transit point; trafficked drugs include cannabis, cocaine, tramadol and ATS precursors (Module 1)
Drug trafficking is a complex, multimillion-dollar criminal business
NDCMP 2015–2019: increased focus on mid- to high-level traffickers and producers — and equal priority to demand reduction and law enforcement
Treatment and continuing-care facilities remain few and inadequate — enforcement alone cannot absorb the problem

lessons.title: How Law Enforcement Often Sees Drug Use
lessons.main:
Agencies predominantly focus on enforcing drug laws and managing the consequences of use
Constant exposure can build very negative attitudes toward illicit drug use
Four categories of drug-related crime connect policing to drug markets: use/distribution offences, income-generating crime, systemic violence, and offences committed under influence

lessons.title: Why Some Officers Resist Public Health Approaches
lessons.main:
Belief that public health responses (including harm reduction) conflict with enforcement goals
Fear that service sites attract users and dealers and disrupt neighbourhoods
Belief that harm reduction compromises prevention and treatment
Concern that not stressing 'Say No To Drugs' zero tolerance might 'increase drug use'
View that interventions for PWID are 'too liberal'
Worry that services for drug users crowd out care for the 'innocent'

lessons.title: The Actual Role — and Unique Position — of Law Enforcement
lessons.main:
Enforce drug laws; ensure everyone lives in a safe, secure environment
Long history of working across public health issues; significant influence on drug strategies
Uniquely placed to steer users to assistance:
Available 24 hours a day, seven days a week
Frequent contact with dependent and problematic users
Contact at ‘treatable moments’ — times of crisis when people are open to change

lessons.title: Best Friend or Worst Enemy
lessons.main:
Law enforcement can be the best friend, or the worst enemy, of a public health response
Unsupportive policing severely disrupts interventions; supportive policing enables them
Active targeting of services leads to: fewer users in services, riskier injecting, users scattering beyond providers' reach, and deep reluctance to engage for fear of arrest
Supportive practice: no unwarranted patrols or searches at service sites; an enabling environment for health and harm reduction work

Knowledge Check

A patrol begins stationing officers outside a drop-in centre and questioning everyone entering. Based on this module, the most likely result is:
A. Attendance rises
B. Users stop attending, disperse and take greater risks — undermining both health and policing goals
C. HIV transmission stops
D. Dealers surrender

Answer: B

lessons.title: Discretion and the Range of Options
lessons.main:
Discretion is not disregard of the law — it weighs the gravity of the ‘crime’, as with minor assaults, theft and traffic offences
Balance accountability (reports, running sheets) against the cost and effort of prosecution
Options for drug use offenders:
Warning — verbal caution, usually undocumented
Caution — formal warning at a station after an offence
Drug diversion — caution conditional on attending clinical assessment and commencing treatment or assistance
Imprisonment is an unhealthy outcome: overcrowding, disease (HIV, hepatitis, TB), violence, abuse and corruption

lessons.title: Making Collaboration Work
lessons.main:
Technical Working Groups of police, health and local government act as multi-sectoral steering committees
Agree strategies from the start; secure management support
Focus on shared benefits and the public image of working together; monitor developments jointly
Kaduna application: the police-to-KADSAMHSA referral and feedback pathway operationalizes exactly this collaboration for eligible cases

lessons.title: Key Points Recap Before Your Case Work
lessons.main:
Law enforcement and public health can — and must — work together
Officers meet people who use drugs at treatable moments no one else sees
Discretion, cautions and diversion beat imprisonment for minor use offences
Supportive policing multiplies the impact of every health investment

lessons.title: Two Scenarios From the Field
lessons.main:
Scenario One: You are posted to a busy station in a low-income area; your supervisor wants to improve public perception of the force. Near the market you see a group of young people; a colleague says some are known drug users — not violent, but deeply mistrustful of officers.
Scenario Two: A 15-year-old boy is brought in for possessing heroin, which he says is for personal use — he injects twice daily. His family is very poor, both parents unemployed; he cannot afford school and his work prospects are limited.

Discuss / respond in the LMS forum:

Scenario One: What action would you take, what biases might shape your interaction, and why might these youths mistrust officers?
Scenario Two: What concerns do you have for the boy's future, what pathways would reduce his drug-related harm and improve his prospects, and what goes in your report?
For both: which ingredients of effective community policing apply — proactive policing, open communication, empathy, role modeling, leadership?
How would a formal referral pathway to KADSAMHSA change your options in Scenario Two?
